newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh ponders MFA end effect on textiles.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh ponders MFA end effect on textiles.

text.p: Bangladesh fears its burgeoning garment sector will face stiff global competition when the international Multifibre Arrangement (MFA) expires in nine years.
"We have to prepare ourselves now to face the competition," Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Thursday.
Hasina said the MFA would be phased out by the year 2005 when a new global trade policy comes into force.
The MFA was concluded in 1973 by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). It lets developed nations offer tariff and import concessions on textiles from developing countries.

"Bangladesh feels it's imperative to strive to maintain the growth in the textile industry to counter competition," Hasina told foreign buyers and local exporters at the opening of the country's annual textile fair.
"The government will offer every assistance to boosting both local and foreign investment in the country's textile sector," Hasina said.

The garment industry accounts for 65 percent of foreign earnings in Bangladesh. Bangladesh in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) earned about US$2.5 billion through garment exports, accounting for some 1.33 percent of the total global trade in clothing.
The bulk of Bangladesh's textile exports go to the U.S. and European Community countries.
The country's 2,800 garment factories are its biggest employer, providing jobs for 1.2 million people, 90 percent of them women.
Commerce Minister Tofael Ahmed said earnings from garment exports might top US$3 billion this year, but lamented the industry's dependence on imported raw materials.

Speaking at the textile fair, Ahmed urged entrepreneurs to set up backyard industries to reduce the cost of imported materials. Local producers meets only five percent of the 2.1 billion yards (metres) used by the garment factories annually.
Hasina said her government, installed in June, had passed laws to let foreign investors set up independent industrial zones in Bangladesh.
"We plan to slowly reduce import duties in accordance with the guidelines set down by the Uruguay Round of the GATT," Hasina said.
She favoured establishment of a fashion institute to further enhance the textile sector, and praised attempts to cut child labour in the industry.
"The country's textile sector has set a pioneering example by sending child labourers to schools," Hasina said.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) are rehabilitating more than 10,500 child workers under a July 1995 agreement.
Bangladesh's garment manufacturers agreed to the terms after the U.S. government threatened to stop importing textiles from countries using workers below the age of 14.

Under the memorandum of understanding reached with the ILO and UNICEF, 130 schools for child labourers have been set up and 2,015 students enrolled. Besides schooling, the children also receive stipends and other assistance.
